Two things you have to realize.

  • The interview starts way before your real interview.
  • The interview is still in progress after you have met the real interview.

 

  • e.g. When you enter the building, the interviewer might have been smoking a cigaret outside the building and saw you entering.
  • e.g. After the interview you might talk about it or feel relieved but on the way out you might pass the secretary of that guy that interviewed you.

Yes! I remember when I was still living at home, my brother came home super angry from an interview. My mom asked what was wrong and it turns out the "Stupid secretary told them not to hire me even though I totally nailed the interview." We didn't have much sympathy for him, even though he really needed the job. There are only so many reasons a secretary would tell their boss not to hire an employee, and it certainly wouldn't be surprising to hear my brother was rude to someone he felt was beneath him. I don't believe he learned a lesson that day, but I sure did.

So true. I got my current job because I picked up a tissue from the floor and put it in the bin while my dead-heat competitor stepped over it. We were so closely tied that that tiny action swung it in my favour.

When you are on an interview, they do not only look at how smart you are or how well you do your job. They will also look at if you actually will fit into the team.

One big issue I have been facing is that they did not hire me because I was smarter than the team leader and he would not like to lose power. The other things is that if you have to work with an older guy, they don't want you to tell them that they are wrong or that you know better.

You may want to change your approach in the interview process then to demonstrate how you influence without having authority. There is a special skill to this, and demonstrating that you can influence up an organization is just as important as whether or not you are able to manage those you supervise.

About telling someone they are wrong and you know better--what person wants to be approached by anyone who comes through with that mentality and demeanor. Even if you don't directly say it, that body language is evident, and will never get anything accomplished. I might suggest reading "How to Win Friends and Influence People" by Dale Carnegie, because you definitely catch more flies with honey.

It all depends on the type of position.

Sometimes they want a bad ass that kicks ass and dare to oppose the rest of the colleagues. Because if you team is full of people that never takes initiative then no work gets done.

Sometimes they need followers because 2 kick ass leaders will only but heads and take down the team.

The hard part is that you cannot predict what they really need. I think you should as the question, what they actually need.
What are the current struggles the department I am applying for is facing and what can a new hire do to help.

• What is career advancement look like in this organization? Or alternatively, how they view and contribute to professional growth of individuals.
  • Who are your biggest competitors, and how are you differentiated and winning?
  • How do you see me as a fit with your team/company?
  • How do I compare to others interviewing for, or who have recently received the job?

Lastly, take a little bit of time to take the research that you have done on the company and turn it into a topical question that shows you have a grasp of the macro world that is going on around you, and how it will impact the nature of your work in the future.

How do I compare to others interviewing for, or who have recently received the job?

So it isn't in bad taste to ask them to compare me to other that may be applying? I'm not sure why, but that makes me mildly uncomfortable. Though I suppose it shouldn't, because that is exactly what they are doing, whether I ask about it or not...

No, it's not in bad taste at all. It gives them an opportunity to tell them about potential concerns they have with you compared to others and you may be able to address that.

Or as happened to me one time, I had a lot better qualifications than the others they were considering. I could have used it for salary negotiation leverage when the time came, but instead it served as sort of a wake up call that I should be seeking a better position, which I sought out and received.

Something a lot of people dont realize (especially with these "adult" jobs) is that the interview is a two way street. The best way to approach this is by doing a little research about the company beforehand. Find out more about ways they might be expanding and more about the history of the company itself. This will give you some "ammunition" during the interview to talk about the company in detail and show that you are an independent thinker and that you've done your "homework". As for questions: Here are a few I've found to be successful.

-What are your responsibilities here at "company X"?

-Does "Company X" have any new upcoming projects or expansions?

-What are "Company X's" strengths and weaknesses compared to its competition?

-What are the day-to-day responsibilities of this job?

• What does an average day look like?
  • Why did you (the employer) chose the job?
  • What do new hires find the hardest/Are there some skills that could benefit me/make the job easier?
  • What do people who work here do after 1-2 years?

"When I was researching the company I didn't notice anything about volunteering. Do any employees get together to volunteer somewhere, and if I'm hired, how would I get involved with that?" Or ask about the social culture, like whether there are opportunities to help put together a basketball game and BBQ, or if a group of employees goes to the gym together before or after work.

Something that makes it seem like you want to get involved with the company, that you're a nice person with well-rounded interests, and you take care of your body.
What will I learn in this job?
They also look for how well you fit into their team so asking about your immediate colleagues interests (and having an interested response) might give you a boost in personable-ness.
